power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.formatted: Smoking intensity showed a dose-response pattern: smoking <20 cigarettes/day was associated with any ER visit (OR 1.130, 95% CI [1.060-1.204]), frequent ER use (OR 1.231, 95% CI [1.124-1.347]), and ER visit count (RR 1.262, 95% CI [1.110-1.435]), while smoking ≥20 cigarettes/day showed stronger associations with any ER visit (OR 1.231,), frequent ER use (OR   1.447,), and ER visit count (RR 1.368,]; all p<0.001).

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Background: Tobacco smoking is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the United States, yet its longitudinal association with emergency room (ER) utilization remains understudied.
We examined whether cigarette smoking, smoking intensity, and smoking trajectories were associated with subsequent ER use.
Methods: We analyzed adult respondents from Waves 1-6 of the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study.
Wave 1-3 smoking status, intensity, and cigarettes/day were examined in relation to next-wave ER outcomes.
Logistic generalized estimating equation models were used for any ER visit and frequent ER use (≥2 visits), and quasi-Poisson models were used for ER visit count.
Trajectory analyses examined Wave 1-5 smoking patterns and Wave 6 ER outcomes, with Wave 1-4 to Wave 5 as sensitivity analysis.
Marginal structural models and propensity score matching were used to strengthen causal interpretation.
Models adjusted for demographics, insurance, self-rated health, and baseline ER use.
Survey weights with balanced repeated replication and Fay's adjustment were used.

Results: In adjusted GEE models, current smoking was associated with higher subsequent ER utilization, including any ER visit (OR 1.128, 95% CI [1.068-1.191]), frequent ER use (OR 1.275,), and ER visit count (RR 1.264,]; all p<0.001).

text.text: Smoking intensity showed a dose-response pattern: smoking <20 cigarettes/day was associated with any ER visit (OR 1.130, 95% CI [1.060-1.204]), frequent ER use (OR 1.231, 95% CI [1.124-1.347]), and ER visit count (RR 1.262, 95% CI [1.110-1.435]), while smoking ≥20 cigarettes/day showed stronger associations with any ER visit (OR 1.231,), frequent ER use (OR   1.447,), and ER visit count (RR 1.368,]; all p<0.001).

text.text: Each additional cigarette/day was also associated with higher ER utilization (OR/RR range, 1.007-1.011; all p<0.001).

text.text: Findings were consistent in marginal structural models and propensity score matched analyses.

In trajectory analyses, new/intermittent and persistent smokers had significantly higher ER utilization, while former/intermittent smokers and sustained quitters did not differ from non-smokers, suggesting that this harmful association was eliminated by smoking cessation.

Conclusions: Smoking, heavier intensity, and persistent or emerging smoking patterns were associated with higher subsequent ER utilization, while smoking cessation reduces ER risk to the same level as non-smokers.
This supports smoking prevention and cessation as strategies to reduce acute healthcare burden.
Smoking should be considered not only a risk factor for long-term chronic disease, but also a predictor of acute healthcare utilization.

The consistency of findings across longitudinal, marginal structural, and propensity score matched analyses supports a potential causal relationship between smoking exposure and subsequent emergency room use.

These results strengthen the rationale for integrating smoking cessation counseling, nicotine replacement therapy, quitline referral, and preventive care linkage into emergency and urgent care settings, alongside broader tobacco-control policies to reduce acute healthcare burden.
Tobacco use remains a major public health burden in the United States and globally.

In the United States, cigarette smoking and secondhand smoke exposure cause more than 480,000 deaths each year, nearly one in five deaths, and cost more than $600 billion in 2018, including more than $240 billion in health care spending (CDC, 2024).

text.text: Although adult cigarette smoking has declined, with 9.9% of U.S. adults reporting current cigarette smoking in 2024 compared with 11.6% in 2022, tobacco-related morbidity remains substantial (CDC, 2024; NCHS, 2026).

text.text: Globally, tobacco causes more than 7 million deaths each year, including more than 1.6 million deaths among nonsmokers exposed to secondhand smoke (WHO, 2026).

text.text: Emergency room (ER) care represents an important but understudied setting for understanding the acute healthcare burden of smoking.
In 2022, the United States had approximately 155.4 million emergency department visits, or 47.3 visits per 100 people (CDC/NCHS, 2024).

National ED visit costs totaled $76.3 billion across 144.8 million visits in 2017, and claims-based data show continued increases in ER spending and prices (Moore & Liang, 2020; Health Care Cost Institute, 2023).
text.formatted: National ED visit costs totaled $76.3 billion across 144.8 million visits in 2017, and claims-based data show continued increases in ER spending and prices <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Moore & Liang, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Health Care Cost Institute, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Smokers may be overrepresented in emergency care; although current smoking prevalence among U.S. adults is below 14%, smokers may account for approximately 30-40% of ED patients (Yale Medicine, n.d.), yet the longitudinal relationship between smoking and ER utilization remains insufficiently characterized.

Prior studies have linked smoking with increased ED utilization, particularly among patients with asthma, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and respiratory disease (Barmparessou et al., 2020; Selya et al., 2020; Madani & Carpenter, 2023).

text.text: Cross-sectional ED studies have also shown that tobacco use is common among ED patients and that the ED may be an important setting for identifying smokers and delivering cessation interventions (Smith, 2011).
text.formatted: Cross-sectional ED studies have also shown that tobacco use is common among ED patients and that the ED may be an important setting for identifying smokers and delivering cessation interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Smith, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: More recent evidence further supports this clinical relevance: smoking has been associated with frequent treatand-release ED visits across health-complexity groups (Castner et al., 2015), and an ED-based ces-sation trial improved 6-month biochemically verified abstinence compared with usual care (Pope et al., 2024).

text.text: However, much of the existing literature remains disease-specific, geographically limited, retrospective, or cross-sectional, limiting generalizability and causal interpretation.

To address these gaps, this study examined the longitudinal association between cigarette smoking and subsequent ER utilization among U.S. adults, including any ER visit, frequent ER use, and ER visit count.

We also evaluated whether smoking intensity and smoking behavior trajectories, including persistent smoking, new/intermittent smoking, former/intermittent smoking, sustained quitting, and relapse, were associated with later ER outcomes.

Using data from the nationally representative Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) Study, this analysis aimed to clarify how smoking status, smoking intensity, and smoking patterns over time relate to acute healthcare utilization.
The PATH Study is a nationally representative longitudinal cohort study of U.S. adults and youth.
The study used a four-stage, stratified, address-based probability sampling design and oversampled adult tobacco users, young adults aged 18-24 years, and Black adults.
Full-sample and replicate weights were created to account for the complex sampling design, oversampling, and nonresponse (Hyland et al., 2017; Opsomer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Full-sample and replicate weights were created to account for the complex sampling design, oversampling, and nonresponse <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hyland et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Opsomer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The primary longitudinal analysis used smoking exposures from Waves 1-3 to predict ER outcomes at the subsequent wave, corresponding to Wave 1 to Wave 2, Wave 2 to Wave 3, and Wave 3 to Wave 4.

Secondary trajectory analyses examined smoking behavior patterns from Waves 1-5 in relation to Wave 6 ER outcomes, with sensitivity analyses using Waves 1-4 smoking patterns to predict Wave 5 ER outcomes during the pre-pandemic period.
Smoking exposure was defined using PATH-derived current established cigarette smoking status and average cigarettes smoked per day.
Current established cigarette smoking was based on the PATH-derived variable R0#R_A_CUR_ESTD_CIGS.

Smoking intensity was categorized among current established smokers as <20 cigarettes/day or ≥20 cigarettes/day using the PATH-derived average cigarettes-per-day variable; non-smokers served as the reference group.
text.formatted: Smoking intensity was categorized among current established smokers as <20 cigarettes/day or ≥20 cigarettes/day using the PATH-derived average cigarettes-per-day variable; non-smokers served as the reference group.

text.text: ER outcomes were based on self-reported emergency room or urgent care use in the past 12 months, including any ER visit (R0#_AX0302), frequent ER use defined as ≥2 visits, and total ER visit count (R0#_AX0155).
For the primary longitudinal analysis, smoking exposures were measured at Waves 1-3 and linked to ER outcomes at the subsequent waves.
For trajectory analyses, smoking patterns were defined across Waves 1-5, with Waves 1-4 used in sensitivity analyses.
Trajectory categories included persistent non-smokers, persistent smokers, former/intermittent smokers, new/intermittent smokers, sustained quitters, and relapsed/intermittent smokers.
Persistent non-smokers were non-smokers at all included waves and served as the reference group.
Persistent smokers were smokers at all included waves.
Former/intermittent smokers were smokers at Wave 1 but were not smokers at all subsequent waves.
New/intermittent smokers were non-smokers at Wave 1 but reported smoking at one or more later waves.
Sustained quitters were Wave 1 smokers who remained non-smokers at all subsequent included waves, and relapsed/intermittent smokers were Wave 1 smokers with mixed smoking status across later waves.
Baseline covariates were selected to capture demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare access, and health-status factors previously associated with tobacco use and ER utilization.
These included age group, sex, race/ethnicity, education, income, insurance status, self-rated physical health, and baseline ER visit count.
Reference groups were age 18-24 years, male sex, White race/ethnicity, 6 less than high school education, income <$10,000, no insurance, and excellent self-rated physical health.

text.text: Education categories included GED, high school graduate, some college/associate degree, bachelor's degree, and advanced degree.
Insurance categories included private insurance, Medicaid, Medicare and other insurance.

Covariates adjusted included prior ER utilization, self-rated health, and sociodemographic factors, including age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, income, and insurance status.
Generalized estimating equation models were used to account for repeated observations within participants (Liang & Zeger, 1986).

text.text: Together, these findings support a persistence-related association between smoking exposure and later ER utilization and highlight the potential impact of smoking cessation in reducing or eliminating the excess ERutilization burden associated with continued smoking.
Because the former/intermittent smoking category may include both sustained quitters and individuals who relapsed, we conducted an additional cessation-focused trajectory analysis.

Sustained quitters were defined as Wave 1 smokers who were non-smokers at all subsequent included waves, while relapsed/intermittent smokers were Wave 1 smokers who were not consistently non-smokers during follow-up.

Sustained quitters (waves 1-5) were not significantly different from persistent non-smokers for any of the three Wave 6 ER outcomes (Supplementary Figure 3A), suggesting that sustained cessation may reduce the excess ER-utilization risk seen among continued smokers.

text.text: The relationship between smoking and emergency room (ER) utilization has received relatively limited attention compared with other substance-use predictors of emergency care, and some prior analyses of ER use and substance use did not directly evaluate cigarette smoking (Capp et al., 2014; Walley et al., 2012).

text.text: To our knowledge, this study is among the first nationally representative longitudinal analyses to examine smoking status, smoking intensity, and smoking trajectories in relation to subsequent ER utilization among U.S. adults.
The use of PATH survey weights and replicate weights allowed us to account for the complex sampling design (Hyland et al., 2017; Opsomer et al., 2024).

text.text: Our repeated-wave structure design further allowed us to evaluate temporal associations, multiple ER outcomes, and smoking trajectories over time rather than relying on a single cross-sectional smoking measure.

Our findings suggest that smoking may contribute to emergency care burden not only by increasing the likelihood of any ER use, but also by increasing recurrent and higher-volume utilization, particularly among heavier smokers.

In adjusted models, current established smoking was associated with a 26.4% higher rate of subsequent ER visits, with higher rates among smokers consuming <20 cigarettes/day and ≥20 cigarettes/day compared with non-smokers.

text.text: The per-cigarette association was modest, but scaled to one pack/day, it corresponded to approximately 20% higher ER visit rates.

Given the high cost of emergency care, these differences may be meaningful at the population level: national estimates suggest that ED visit costs totaled $76.3 billion across 144.8 million visits in 2017, and more recent claims-based data show continued increases in ER spending and prices (Moore & Liang, 2020; Health Care Cost Institute, 2023).

text.text: These findings suggest that reducing smoking exposure may have implications beyond long-term chronic disease prevention, potentially lowering recurrent acute-care use and its associated healthcare burden.
These findings are consistent with prior evidence linking tobacco use to greater acute healthcare utilization.

text.text: Together, these studies consistently support our finding.

Our trajectory findings suggest that both persistent smoking and new/intermittent smoking are associated with higher later ER utilization, supporting the importance of repeated smoking exposure over time rather than a single baseline smoking measure.
This pattern is consistent with trajectorybased studies showing that sustained smoking exposure is associated with cumulative health risk.

In a Korean cohort of 60,709 young men with smoking measured seven times, very-high steady smokers had a 49% higher risk of ASCVD than low-steady smokers, with higher risks of ischemic heart disease (HR 1.63), total stroke (HR 1.36), and ischemic stroke (HR 1.58) (Jee et al., 2019).

text.text: Similarly, in a population-based cohort of 2,448,548 men with smoking measured across four waves, steady heavy smokers had higher cancer incidence (HR 1.53, 95% CI [1.49-1.58]) and cancer mortality (HR 2.64, 95% CI [2.50-2.79]) than steady non-smokers (Luu et al., 2022).

text.text: The elevated ER utilization among new/intermittent smokers in our study may reflect smoking initiation, re-initiation, or unstable smoking behavior, suggesting that even emerging or intermittent smoking exposure may contribute to acute-care burden.
This is consistent with prior evidence linking active smoking, smoking relapse, and smoking-related disease burden with higher ED and healthcare utilization (Baliunas et al., 2023; Kao et al., 2019).

text.text: In contrast, former/intermittent smokers and sustained quitters were not significantly different from persistent non-smokers in later ER utilization, suggesting that stopping smoking may attenuate the excess risk seen among persistent and new/intermittent smokers.

This interpretation is supported by evidence that cessation reduces smoking-related morbidity over time and that healthcare utilization among former smokers may move closer to never-smoker patterns than current-smoker patterns (Fishman et al., 2003; U.S. Surgeon General, 2020) These are crucial factors for emergency department use, with higher acute-care use in primary care shortage areas and lower use where clinic density or urgent care access is greater (Patel et al., 2024; Mathison et al., 2013), which helps clarify whether the association between smoking and ER usage reflects smoking behavior itself or broader social disadvantage.

text.text: Additionally, although the repeated-wave design supports temporal ordering, residual confounding and reverse causation remain possible.

ER use is also a nonspecific outcome: visits may reflect smoking-related illness, but may also be due to accidents, injuries, abdominal pain, acute respiratory infections, headaches, or other conditions not directly attributable to smoking (HCUP, 2018).
Finally, smoking behavior and ER utilization were self-reported, which may introduce recall, perception, or reporting bias.
Smoking, heavier smoking intensity, and persistent or emerging smoking patterns were associated with higher subsequent emergency room (ER) utilization across multiple outcomes.

Together, these findings suggest that sustained smoking exposure increases later ER burden, whereas cessation may reduce this excess burden toward the level observed among persistent non-smokers.
Our findings support integrating evidence-based tobacco cessation into routine clinical care, including ER and urgent care encounters.

The USPSTF recommends that clinicians ask all adults about tobacco use, advise them to stop, and provide behavioral interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for cessation (U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, 2021).

In acute-care settings, brief bedside counseling, nicotine replacement therapy initiation, and quitline referral may provide feasible opportunities to reach smokers who may otherwise have limited access to preventive care (CDC, 2024).

At the policy level, comprehensive tobacco-control programs, smoke-free laws, tobacco price increases, and mass-reach health communication campaigns remain recommended strategies to reduce smoking prevalence and smoking-related morbidity (Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2024).
Despite the novel findings, the study is not without limitations.
Public-use PATH data often lack granular geographic location measures.

If ZIP code or census-tract information were available, future work could incorporate SES measures such as the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) (CDC/ATSDR, 2026) by linking with SDOH datasets.

Restricted geographic data could also enable linkage to local healthcare access measures, including primary care provider density, urgent care availability, federally qualified health centers, rural health clinics, and hospital/ER proximity.
